lesson.heading: Four problems, and what to say
lesson.text: Something will go wrong in almost every interview. What is marked is not the problem but how you handle it - and staying silent is the one response that gives you no credit at all.

examples.note: *I'm not really sure what you mean.*
*I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?*
*I've never really thought about that before.* / *I honestly have no idea.*

lesson.note: Don't be too shy to ask for help in the interview if you need it. Correcting yourself out loud is evidence of control, not a mark against you.

lesson.heading: Responses to a problem

left.label: Lowers your mark
examples: The candidate attempts an answer but is very hesitant.

right.label: Keeps your mark
examples: The candidate asks a question to check.
The candidate corrects him or herself.

lesson.note: Silence gives the examiner nothing to assess. A question or a correction is more language, not less.

lesson.heading: Pronunciation has three parts
lesson.text: The fourth criterion is **Pronunciation**, and it covers more than individual sounds.

examples.note: Hearing the difference is the first step to saying it: *it / eat*, *full / fool*, *board / bird*, *knee / near*, *breathe / breeze*, *save / shave*.

examples.text: Using **intonation and stress** to help communicate your ideas.
examples.note: Good intonation stops your speech sounding monotonous.

examples.text: **Chunking** - running your words together naturally and clearly, not in a robotic way.

lesson.heading: Three ways to say -ed
lesson.note: Word endings matter as much as word beginnings: a swallowed *-ed* can turn a past tense into a present one in the examiner's ear.

lesson.heading: Stress does two jobs
lesson.text: Within a word, stress is part of pronouncing it correctly. Across a sentence, stress adds **emphasis** and extra meaning. The `//` marks below show where a speaker naturally pauses - that is chunking.

examples.text: *Over the years // I've interviewed **hundreds** of candidates // for jobs at many different levels. //*
examples.note: The stressed word carries the point of the sentence.

examples.text: *The point of every job interview is to make sure a candidate has the **skills necessary** to do the work.*

lesson.note: A good way to practise is to play a Listening recording quietly and read the script aloud over it, keeping the speaker's timing and intonation.

lesson.heading: What an examiner actually writes
lesson.text: Saida scored **5.5** overall. Her report shows how specific the assessment is - and what would raise each band.

examples.text: **Fluency and Coherence - 5.** *Slow speech and frequent hesitation. A range of spoken discourse markers (well; so; it depends; actually; I think so; first of all).*

**Lexical Resource - 5.5.** *Some good vocabulary (architectural design, last two decades, cooperative and tolerant) but limited flexibility: repetition of certain items and inappropriacies (it's very actual, some cookings and housekeeping works, she always says me).*

**Grammatical Range and Accuracy - 5.5.** *Quite accurate on basic forms, but little range. Some good complex forms, but most involve infinitive structures. Errors (technology nowdays are really go fast, she become healthy, they are more closer) do not impede communication.*

**Pronunciation - 6.** *Slow speech interferes with chunking and rhythm and she has a problem with 'th'. But control is variable, and when more confident she demonstrates good rhythm and chunking, and some good use of intonation and stress.*

lesson.note: Notice the pattern: she is not marked down for lacking words, but for **range and flexibility** - repeating what she has instead of reaching further.

lesson.text: Record yourself being interviewed, on video if you can, and assess your own performance against the four criteria. If you are unsure which sounds you get wrong, read a passage aloud and ask someone to write down what they hear.

exercises.prompt: Sort these responses to a problem in the interview.

items.text: The candidate is very hesitant throughout
The candidate asks a question to check
The candidate corrects him or herself

exercises.prompt: How is the -ed ending pronounced in each word?
What does *chunking* mean in the Pronunciation criterion?
options: Speaking as fast as you can
Running your words together naturally rather than robotically
Pausing after every word so each one is clear
exercises.explanation: Natural grouping of words - with pauses in sensible places - makes you sound far more fluent than raw speed does.

exercises.prompt: Which syllable is stressed in *expensive*? Write the word with the stressed syllable in capitals: ex___sive.
exercises.explanation: ex-**PEN**-sive. Compare *EN-vi-ronment* and *TECH-nique*, where the stress falls elsewhere.

exercises.statement: Correcting yourself out loud during the Speaking test counts against you.
exercises.explanation: It shows control of the language. Staying silent is the response that gives the examiner nothing to assess.

exercises.prompt: Saida's Lexical Resource was marked 5.5. According to the examiner, what mainly held it back?
options: She used no good vocabulary at all
Limited flexibility - repetition of certain items and some inappropriate uses
She spoke too fast to be understood
She gave answers that were too long
exercises.explanation: She had good vocabulary (*architectural design*, *cooperative and tolerant*) but reused it instead of reaching further.

exercises.prompt: Match each pair of words that are easy to confuse.
Build a phrase to use when you have not heard the examiner.
exercises.answer: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?
exercises.explanation: Polite, complete and instant. Have it ready so it does not cost you thinking time on the day.

exercises.statement: Good intonation stops your speech from sounding monotonous.
exercises.explanation: It is part of the Pronunciation criterion: intonation and stress are how you add meaning beyond the words themselves.
